## Lagrangian development guide

This repository owns the native Lagrangian app, project profiles, preview lifecycle, packaging, and documentation. Compilation and preview rendering are supplied by the maintained tinymist engine or a compatible external executable.

## Layout

- `apps/macos/sources.json`: one source list for native app packaging and tests.
- `apps/macos/`: profile models, settings, project/service control, engine launch, CLI and AppKit composition in separate files.
- `apps/macos/tail-hosting.patch`: optional lifecycle adapter for Tail Hosting.
- `scripts/flow-app.py`: staged app builds, signing, installation, rollback, and migration.
- `tests/flow-app/`: app and packaging tests.
- `assets/branding/`: app branding.
- `docs/tinymist/`: canonical Typst sources.
- `openspec/changes/rename-product-lagrangian/`: current product identity and migration work.
- `crates/`: engine implementations and supporting libraries.
- `tools/reader-common/`: renderer-independent feature policy and state.
- `tools/typst-preview-frontend/` and `tools/typst-dom/`: paged reader adapters and document rendering.
- `tools/flow-reader/flow_reader/`: HTML Reader compiler, document, rendering, services and HTTP packages.
- `tools/flow-reader/web/features/` and `web/rendering/`: HTML Reader feature adapters and semantic rendering.
- `editors/`: editor integrations and tooling.

## Reader architecture

Read [the reader architecture source map](tinymist/dev/reader-architecture.typ) and scoped `AGENTS.md` files before adding reader features. Shared feature policy depends on explicit renderer operations; DOM positions, page coordinates and transport remain with their concrete adapters. The source map also describes compiler and native app ownership.

## Design principles

This guide is the canonical design policy for contributors and agents. Root `AGENTS.md` provides the working entrypoint; scoped instructions add local ownership, contracts and verification. Keep detailed file ownership in the architecture source map and behavior requirements in OpenSpec.

Apply OOP through encapsulated responsibilities and state, with composition preferred over inheritance. Rust traits, Swift protocols, injected functions and classes are all valid tools; choose the simplest idiomatic implementation.

- **Single responsibility:** keep a policy and its invariants with one owner. UI handlers gather inputs and delegate service operations; initialization composes controllers. Separate responsibilities that change for different reasons.
- **Open/closed:** extend an existing feature through its supported operations when a real variation exists. Do not create speculative plugin layers or empty base classes; an existing owner can still be corrected or simplified.
- **Substitution:** implementations of the same contract preserve accepted inputs, outputs, errors, effects and lifetime. Cancellation, stale results and disposal are part of that contract. Test interchangeable adapters against shared behavior.
- **Interface segregation:** expose only the operations each consumer needs. Model unsupported capabilities explicitly instead of requiring dummy methods or inventing page coordinates for semantic DOM positions.
- **Dependency inversion:** policy accepts explicit operations for platform, transport and storage work. Shared reader policy never imports concrete readers; concrete composition wires the dependencies.

Centralize identical policy and mutable-state ownership within the appropriate boundary. Reuse the existing owner before adding another implementation. Similar syntax alone does not justify merging distinct behavior. Cross-language systems share protocol contracts and fixtures rather than an unnecessary universal runtime.

Minimal code means fewer unnecessary states, branches and indirect layers while remaining readable and testable. Extract an abstraction for an actual repeated policy or current extension need. Avoid catch-all utility modules and global service objects. File length, class count and interface count are not measures of SOLID compliance.

## Engine input

Keep engine executables outside the managed source tree. Packaging chooses `--engine` first, then `FLOW_ENGINE_PATH`, then `~/Applications/Lagrangian.app/Contents/MacOS/flow-engine` (falling back to the former `tinymist-flow.app` while migrating). The build copies and signs the supplied executable; use `--build-engine --jobs 2` to build the engine from this workspace before packaging instead. The engine version and input hash identify the dependency independently of the Lagrangian source commit.

A compatible engine supports document preview, device theme variants, `TINYMIST_PREVIEW_FOCUS_FILE`, `TINYMIST_PREVIEW_CHANGE_FILE`, and `TINYMIST_ALLOWED_ORIGINS`. The CLI probe requires `--follow-system-theme`; retain the current installed Flow engine when preserving these features. A different engine needs compatibility verification before use.

HTML Reader services also require the engine’s `source-history` command for project-owned saved-edit observation. Select this executable separately from the HTML compiler with `--engine` or `FLOW_ENGINE_PATH`. The common project store serializes source and renderer metadata updates across processes; HTML-only sessions do not depend on a running paged preview.

## Build and validate

macOS, the Swift compiler, and Python 3 are required for the app. AppKit and Foundation provide the runtime.

```sh
python3 scripts/flow-app.py build --engine /absolute/path/to/flow-engine
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/flow-app -v
python3 scripts/flow-app.py verify dist/Lagrangian.app
```

Tests compile the current Swift sources with warnings treated as errors. Test profiles and update-recovery fixtures use temporary directories. Optional packaging and preview integration tests use `FLOW_TEST_ENGINE` to select an external executable.

Build into `dist`; use the installer for an installed app. Keep installed engines independent of build output. Verify actual document delivery after a release installation, then tag confirmed versions as `flow-vX.Y.Z`.

## Engine and preview development

Use Yarn dependencies for frontend work and the workspace Rust toolchain in the execution environment described under **Remote Rust builds**. With the formatter already installed, formatting checks can run locally:

```sh
yarn install --immutable
node scripts/build.mjs build:preview
cargo fmt --check --all
yarn workspace typst-preview-frontend test run
```

The native engine build uses the locked `flow-release` profile with ThinLTO. `python3 scripts/flow-app.py build --build-engine --jobs 2` compiles Rust and requires a macOS build host. The `flow-engine` GitHub Actions workflow is that host; see **Remote Rust builds**. Running the command on the local Mac requires an explicit local-build instruction. The app manifest records its target, profile, Rust flags and any LTO override in addition to engine version and hashes. On Apple Silicon, use a native ARM Python environment.

## Remote Rust builds

Agent-run Rust compilation requires a Cloud environment explicitly configured for the private `kimpossible-TY/Lagrangian` repository. The former published `tinymist-flow` environment targeted a deleted repository and is not a valid source of truth unless it is reconfigured and its checkout is verified. A request to build or validate Rust authorizes delegating that work to a verified environment, inspecting its progress and retrieving its results. This policy includes Cargo build, check, test, Clippy, bench, doc, run and source-based tool installation, and scripts that invoke Rust compilation, including native engine and browser compiler builders. Local Rust compilation requires an explicit instruction to build locally for that run. If Cloud access is unavailable, report the missing connection and keep the build pending; do not silently fall back to the local Mac.

Use connected task tools to find a matching Cloud build task for Lagrangian. Reuse it only when idle and safe to update; otherwise start an isolated task in the verified environment. Where task tools are unavailable, configure a Cloud environment for the private repository before dispatch. A local task can continue editing source and delegate just its Rust validation. These instructions guide agents; they do not redirect a manually entered terminal `cargo build` command.

Before dispatch, identify the requested commit and any uncommitted source that must be included. Transfer that exact source through an authorized path. Do not commit or push unrelated changes, discard local changes, or claim that an older GitHub checkout validates newer local source. The Cloud task must verify its checkout SHA, preserve Rust toolchain and lockfile requirements, prepare assets with the saved environment setup, and run the smallest affected checks.

In the prepared Cloud checkout, the basic engine verification is:

```sh
. /workspace/.cloud-tools/env.sh
git rev-parse HEAD
RUSTFLAGS=-Dwarnings cargo build --locked --bin tinymist
RUSTFLAGS=-Dwarnings cargo test --locked -p tinymist-preview --lib
RUSTFLAGS=-Dwarnings cargo test --locked -p tinymist-std --no-default-features --lib
target/debug/tinymist --version
```

Retain dependency and build caches in Cloud. Await the actual job result and report the checked SHA, commands, exit statuses and test results; submission alone is not a successful build. Local Git operations, source inspection, preinstalled formatters, JavaScript checks and prebuilt Typst/typlite tools can still run locally without rebuilding Rust caches.

The configured Cloud environment produces Linux binaries. A Linux build does not validate or supply a macOS executable. Native macOS artifacts are built by the `flow-engine` GitHub Actions workflow on an Apple Silicon `macos-latest` runner. Local app packaging reuses that executable with `--engine`.

`.github/workflows/flow-engine.yml` is the only GitHub Actions workflow. It runs on every push to `main` and when someone dispatches it (`workflow_dispatch`). It does not run on pull requests. A push that only changes `docs/**`, `openspec/**`, or Markdown does not start the job. Dispatch it on the same ref that `fetch-engine --branch` will search: a run started with `--ref main` is a successful run for `--branch main`. Push runs are included because `fetch-engine` does not filter on the event.

Before building, the job hashes engine inputs: Rust sources, every `Cargo.toml` and `Cargo.lock`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, the scripts the workflow uses to stage assets and build, the preview and localization sources those scripts embed, other crate and vendor inputs, and the runner OS and architecture. It looks through the newest successful runs on `main`, and on the current ref when that ref is not `main`, for a retained artifact with that hash. The hash is a separate artifact named `flow-engine-input-<hash>`. The artifact `fetch-engine` downloads stays `flow-engine-darwin-arm64`. Its files stay the unsigned `flow-engine`, `flow-engine.sha256`, `release.json` (including `engineBuild`), and `Lagrangian.app`.

On a hit, the job downloads that engine artifact and uploads it again without running Cargo, Yarn, or the Swift packaging. The engine SHA-256 matches the earlier build. `release.json` still records the commit that produced those bytes, which can be older than the run `fetch-engine` selects. On a miss, the job checks out full git history so the engine version can embed `git describe`, installs the toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml`, and caches Cargo through `actions-rust-lang/setup-rust-toolchain` (Swatinem/rust-cache) under the shared key `flow-release-aarch64-apple-darwin`, together with the toolchain and `Cargo.lock`. After `yarn install --frozen-lockfile`, the job runs `node scripts/stage-tinymist-assets.mjs` with no arguments. That prepares the gitignored preview page and copies the committed localization catalog without compiling Rust. The job then runs `python3 scripts/flow-app.py build --build-engine --jobs 2` with `RUSTFLAGS=-Dwarnings`. That is the only Rust compilation in the job, and it uses the locked `flow-release` profile with ThinLTO. The runner must be `arm64`. Staging checks `tinymist --version` and `preview --help` for `--follow-system-theme`, then uploads `flow-engine-darwin-arm64` for 30 days. The dispatch accepts a `jobs` input; the default is 2. A later run for the same ref cancels the older in-progress run. The job token keeps `actions: write` because publishing the artifact, downloading a previous artifact, and saving the Cargo cache need it. A matching artifact older than the 30-day retention, or outside the newest 30 successful runs on each searched branch, is a miss and builds again. A hit republishes the previous `Lagrangian.app` as well, so Swift, branding, and the bundled user-guide PDF stay with the engine build that produced them.

The minimum supported Rust is `rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`. The workflow installs `channel` from `rust-toolchain.toml`. Keep them on the same release: channel `1.92` matches `rust-version = "1.92"`. `yarn check-msrv` used to compare `rust-version` with the `# check-min-version` toolchain pin in `ci.yml`. That workflow and script are gone, so compare the two files directly. This check does not compile Rust.

On the Mac, download a successful run and package with the printed engine path. `fetch-engine` only downloads, verifies, and prints that path:

```sh
gh auth status
engine=$(python3 scripts/flow-app.py fetch-engine --branch main)
python3 scripts/flow-app.py build --engine "$engine"
```

`fetch-engine` uses `gh run list` for the latest successful `flow-engine.yml` run on that branch. Manual runs are included because `workflow_dispatch` is recorded on the ref given to `--ref`. Pass `--run-id <id>` to select one run. The download is stored in `~/Library/Caches/Lagrangian/engines/<run-id>/`, outside the repository `target/` directory. The command checks the SHA-256 against `flow-engine.sha256` and `release.json`, clears the macOS quarantine attribute, probes `--version` and `--follow-system-theme`, and prints the absolute engine path. Pass that path to `--engine`. The same directory also contains `release.json` and the ad-hoc signed `Lagrangian.app` from the runner; local packaging uses the printed `flow-engine` so the installed app keeps the Mac signing identity.

```sh
engine=$(python3 scripts/flow-app.py fetch-engine --run-id 123456789)
python3 scripts/flow-app.py build --engine "$engine"
```

`gh workflow run` requires this file on the default branch. The `--ref` argument is the branch `fetch-engine --branch` searches:

```sh
gh workflow run flow-engine.yml --ref main
```

## Documentation

Edit Typst sources, then regenerate the Markdown outputs. The generator uses an external `typlite` executable from PATH or `TYPLITE_BIN`. Prebuilt typlite executables are available from the [Tinymist releases](https://github.com/Myriad-Dreamin/tinymist/releases). Node.js supports this generator, and Node.js with Yarn is required for preview frontend and editor work.

```sh
node scripts/link-docs.mjs
node scripts/link-docs.mjs --check
typst compile --root . docs/tinymist/flow-app.typ dist/UserGuide.pdf
```

`README.md`, `docs/dev-guide.md`, and `docs/tinymist/flow-app.md` are generated. The web user guide and bundled PDF share `docs/tinymist/flow-app.typ`; edit that source once, then regenerate Markdown and rebuild the app to update its PDF. Images and local links in the Typst sources use source-relative paths; the generator rebases them for each Markdown output. `--readme-only` limits generation or checking to the README.

The [web user guide](tinymist/flow-app.md) describes the first preview and reading actions. The [reading demo](tinymist/examples/reading-demo.typ) supplies a small, theme-aware document for trying those actions. `docs/tinymist/images/mobile-selection.png` is a screenshot of that demo in the actual preview frontend at a phone-sized touch viewport. Capture it with an isolated preview and focus record when the demo or selection UI changes. App sources compile independently of documentation conversion tools.

## Workflow

Continue on the current branch unless the user requests another. Use Conventional Commits per work item. Read `openspec/config.yaml`, accepted specs and matching active changes for new features, observable behavior/contract changes and refactors across responsibility boundaries. Continue matching active work and keep proposal, design, tasks and spec deltas aligned. Small local fixes and documentation-only edits can proceed under existing contracts without a new change.

Preserve unrelated changes and upstream notices; record intentionally imported upstream commits. Keep version/dependency/release edits scoped to actual needs. PR descriptions list modified features and issue operations without execution logs. Development tests/builds use isolated profiles and must not install or restart the user’s services. Releases use a clean commit, bundled installation and verified document delivery before a `flow-vX.Y.Z` tag.

## Validation policy

Keep behavior tests beside their feature owner. Policy tests cover state transitions and failure recovery; contract tests cover supported inputs, errors, cancellation, stale responses and disposal; integration tests cover real compiler/browser/service and installed-layout delivery. Share contract fixtures only for implementations with the same semantics.

Use code review for responsibility, reuse and abstraction decisions. Automate objective boundaries with lint, type checks and dependency tests. The existing `tools/reader-common/tests/architecture.mjs` checks cross-reader imports and runtime cycles. Do not replace behavioral assertions with source-text or line-count tests.

Commands below run from the repository root. Start with the affected scope and widen for consumers when shared contracts change:

- Rust: `RUSTFLAGS=-Dwarnings cargo test -p <crate> --locked`, crate Clippy and `cargo fmt --check --all`. Public facade changes also compile consumers. Broad changes use workspace tests/Clippy; feature combinations use `scripts/feature-testing.sh`. Preserve workspace documentation and safety lints. Inspect analyzer snapshot diffs before explicitly accepting expected changes.
- JavaScript/TypeScript: `yarn lint` aggregates `lint:vscode` and `lint:readers`. Reader lint rejects warnings and separates browser globals from Node globals; vendor/generated files are excluded. Existing VS Code rules retain their baseline until warnings are separately assessed. Use affected project type checks and formatting checks as well.
- Reader boundaries: `yarn test:architecture`. Shared policy changes: `yarn test:readers` includes shared/HTML Node tests, Python services, paged frontend, DOM tests, and installed-layout tests. Build changes also require `yarn build:preview`.
- Python: `yarn test:reader-services` runs the existing service/install suite. Compiler fixtures need `FLOW_READER_PACKAGES` and optionally `FLOW_READER_TYPST`. `yarn test:reader-integration` requires the package directory and rejects all skipped tests; use macOS with Neovim and set `TAIL_HOSTING_SOURCE` to the companion source checkout for the complete suite. Python lint adoption requires a separate baseline assessment.
- Native app: `yarn flow:test` compiles Swift with warnings as errors and exercises service recovery, packaging, and isolated `migrate-tail-hosting` / `restore-tail-hosting` round-trips for `typst-always-preview`, `typst-reader`, and background-manager LaunchAgents (including `--dry-run`, SHA-256 verification, and port-conflict checks). Set `FLOW_TEST_ENGINE` for external-engine coverage.
- VS Code: use the scoped instructions for unit, LSP integration and system/web bundle checks. Grammar changes use `yarn test:grammar`.
- Documentation: regenerate with `node scripts/link-docs.mjs`, then run `yarn docs:check` and compile the changed Typst source.

Local checks use these package scripts. The base reader suite can report skipped optional compiler/editor fixtures; it does not prove browser or physical-device coverage. Required integration runs must provision prerequisites and fail rather than silently skip. Browser fixtures assert their own compiler and Playwright prerequisites; native terminal and physical-device checks remain separate. When moving assets, verify imports, build inputs, static routes and the installed layout, then generate new release artifacts without rewriting immutable releases.

Report checks actually run and skipped coverage. Do not broaden testing after relevant checks pass unless the change or new evidence warrants it.
